c.tagline: Cambodia's riverside capital of golden pagodas and poignant history.

taxi.fareNote: There is no metered street-taxi fleet; get around by tuk-tuk or car booked through the Grab or PassApp apps, which show an upfront fixed fare. Street tuk-tuks and motos have no meter, so agree the price before you set off. US dollars are accepted everywhere alongside riel.

emergency.note: 119 reaches an ambulance and 118 the fire service, but response can be slow; the Tourist Police (012 942 484) handle visitor issues, and private hospitals often dispatch their own ambulances faster.

avoid.reason: Motorbike bag-snatching (esp. the riverside) and phone theft — wear bags cross-body away from the road; petty theft

hood_desc: The historic riverside heart along Sisowath Quay where the Tonle Sap meets the Mekong, home to the Royal Palace, Silver Pagoda, National Museum, and Wat Phnom; the walkable, most convenient base for first-timers, lined with riverfront restaurants and bars.

Phnom Penh's leafy, upmarket expat and embassy district just south of the Independence Monument, packed with the city's best international restaurants, cafes, wine bars, and boutique hotels; ideal for travelers who want comfort, dining, and nightlife within walking distance.

A trendy, increasingly bohemian neighborhood built around the sprawling Russian Market (Tuol Tom Poung), famous for silverware, silk, and bargain finds, now ringed by hip third-wave cafes, tailors, and design shops; suits shoppers and creatives after a more local, less touristy vibe.

A quieter peninsula across the river where the Tonle Sap and Mekong join, offering riverfront promenades, sunset views back over the skyline, and newer residential developments; a calmer, more residential base a short tuk-tuk ride from the center.

A lively riverside district south of the Royal Palace anchored by the NagaWorld casino complex, the AEON Mall, and the buzzing Bassac Lane cocktail-bar alley; a go-to for dining, drinking, and nightlife.

water.note: The city's tap water is treated to a high standard, but most visitors stick to bottled.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 5:30am to 8:30pm daily; after that, tuk-tuks and ride apps are the only option.
transit.note: Phnom Penh has no metro, tram, or urban rail. A modest public city-bus network covers main roads, but tuk-tuks (hailed on the street or via PassApp/Grab) are how nearly everyone gets around.
transit.pay: City buses cost a flat 1,500 riel (about US$0.40), paid in cash to the conductor on board; there is no rechargeable transit card. Most visitors skip the buses and get around by tuk-tuk booked on PassApp or Grab, paying in the app or cash.

landmarks: Royal Palace of Cambodia
This dazzling walled complex of gilded spires and traditional Khmer architecture has served as the king's residence since 1866 and remains the city's crown jewel.
Silver Pagoda
Named for its 5,000 silver floor tiles, this ornate temple within the Royal Palace grounds houses a dazzling emerald Buddha and a life-size gold Buddha statue.
Wat Phnom
Perched atop the city's only hill, this legendary hilltop pagoda gave Phnom Penh its name and remains a lively spot for locals seeking blessings and fortune.
Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum
A former high school turned Khmer Rouge prison (S-21), this haunting museum preserves cells and photographs that confront visitors with Cambodia's tragic recent history.
Choeung Ek Killing Fields
A somber memorial site with a towering glass stupa filled with skulls, marking the mass graves where thousands perished under the Khmer Rouge regime.
National Museum of Cambodia
Housed in a striking terracotta-red traditional building, this museum showcases the world's finest collection of Khmer sculpture, from Angkor-era stone deities to bronzes.
Independence Monument
A lotus-inspired sandstone tower modeled on Angkor Wat's spires, illuminated at night, commemorating Cambodia's 1953 independence from French colonial rule.
Sisowath Quay (Riverside)
A bustling promenade along the confluence of the Tonle Sap and Mekong rivers, packed with cafes, sunset strollers, and views of passing river life.
Wat Ounalom
The former headquarters of Cambodian Buddhism, this riverside pagoda complex of stupas and shrines is said to house a relic of the Buddha's eyebrow.
Central Market (Phsar Thmei)
An Art Deco masterpiece with a soaring yellow dome and four wings radiating outward, this 1937 market remains a vibrant hub for gems, food, and souvenirs.

train.note: Phnom Penh's Royal Railway station stands at the western end of Preah Monivong Boulevard, walkable from the centre. Two lines radiate out: the southern line to Takeo, Kampot, Kep and Sihanoukville (about 7 hours) and the northern line to Pursat, Battambang and on towards Poipet, plus a shuttle to the airport. Services have run at reduced frequency, often only at weekends and holidays, so check before relying on them; tickets are sold at the station and through BookMeBus (https://www.bookmebus.com/). Cambodia has no through international passenger trains - the Poipet track is joined to Thailand's network but only freight and empty stock cross, so travellers change to a bus or taxi at the border.

bus.note: Phnom Penh has no central bus station - each company departs from its own office, with Mekong Express, Phnom Penh Sorya, Capitol Tours and GST clustered near the Central Market, and Giant Ibis just north of the night market. Vietnamese operators such as Danh Danh and Kumho load on Samdech Preah Sihanouk Boulevard south of the Olympic Stadium. Ho Chi Minh City takes 6-7 hours for US$22-25 with the crew handling the paperwork at Bavet, Bangkok is 11-13 hours for US$15-26, and Vientiane needs a change or two and about 27 hours. Vietnam requires a visa or e-visa arranged before you travel; Cambodian re-entry visas are issued at the land borders.

intl.to: Chau Doc (Vietnam) - speedboat down the Bassac / Mekong from the tourist pier on Sisowath Quay, 4-5 hr
intl.op: Hang Chau Speedboat — tickets through Phnom Penh travel agents and guesthouses

ferry.note: The Mekong boats leave from the tourist pier on Sisowath Quay in the centre, and the Chau Doc run is a genuine international crossing with immigration formalities handled on the riverbank - Hang Chau's fast boat takes about 4 hours, while Victoria and Mandarin run slower, pricier tourist boats of about 5 hours. You need a Vietnamese visa or e-visa in advance, as the river post does not issue them. The old fast boat up the Tonle Sap to Siem Reap has not operated since the pandemic, so the only way north by water is the seasonal Battambang - Siem Reap service. Book a day ahead through a guesthouse or agent; there is no walk-up ticket office at the pier.

half.name: Koh Dach
half.blurb: Mekong River island reached by a short ferry ride is dotted with weaving villages producing traditional Khmer silk on wooden looms.

half.name: Udong
half.blurb: Former royal capital about 40 km north holds a ridge of stupas and pagodas overlooking rice paddies from before Phnom Penh became the capital.

half.name: Phnom Chisor
half.blurb: Hilltop Angkorian temple roughly 55 km south requires a steep staircase climb and looks out over flat Cambodian countryside.

full.name: Kirirom National Park
full.blurb: Pine-forested plateau about 110 km southwest offers cooler mountain air, waterfalls and viewpoints over the Cardamom foothills.
